opus-5.5.text:
Well, if you think about it from first principles, I think those are the two that ultimately scale to what civilization is going to need, especially once you factor in things like AI and the energy demands that come with it.

Solar, in a sense, is already fusion. It's just fusion happening at a safe distance, ninety-three million miles away. The sun is this incredible free reactor in the sky, and the costs of photovoltaics have come down dramatically, faster than almost anyone predicted. The remaining challenges are mostly engineering ones: storage, grid infrastructure, materials efficiency. Those are exactly the kinds of problems where I think AI can help a lot, for example designing better battery chemistries or new materials for more efficient panels.

Fusion is the other side of that coin. If we can get it working on Earth, it's essentially clean, abundant, baseload energy, with fuel you can get from seawater. And I've been quite involved in thinking about this, partly because we did work at DeepMind with collaborators on using reinforcement learning to control the plasma in a tokamak. Holding a plasma stable at those temperatures is an extraordinarily hard control problem, and it's the kind of thing learning systems turn out to be quite good at. There are also materials problems, like what lines the reactor walls, where AI-driven discovery could speed things up.

The reason I find this exciting is what it unlocks downstream. If energy becomes essentially free and clean, so many other problems change character. Desalination becomes cheap, so water scarcity eases. You can do carbon capture at scale. Manufacturing, even things like making rocket fuel, all of that shifts. So many of the hard constraints we face today are really energy constraints underneath.

So my bet is that over the next decade or two, AI helps us crack the remaining science and engineering on both fronts. That could move us toward what I sometimes call radical abundance, where we're no longer in a zero-sum world fighting over scarce resources. That's one of the most hopeful things I think this technology could contribute to.

r001.rationale: It explicitly names storage as one of the remaining engineering challenges for solar power.

r002.rationale: It names grid infrastructure as a solar challenge, which communicates the need to build out electricity transmission.

r003.rationale: It describes the challenge of holding plasma stable and using learning systems to control it, but does not communicate that control must be sufficiently fast.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think if you look at it from first principles, the sun is this enormous fusion reactor that's already been running for billions of years, and it's pouring vastly more energy onto the Earth every hour than humanity uses in a year. So in a sense, solar is just the near-term way of tapping into fusion that already exists. And then fusion itself, if we can crack it here on Earth, is essentially unlimited clean energy with fuel that's abundant, you know, isotopes of hydrogen from seawater, and no long-lived waste, no carbon. Those two together look to me like the physics-level answer to energy, rather than a stopgap.

The reason I'm optimistic, and why I'd bet on them, is that both of them are fundamentally problems that AI can help with. Solar is a materials science problem, better photovoltaics, better batteries, room-temperature superconductors for transmission if we ever get there. And those are exactly the kinds of search problems, huge combinatorial spaces of possible materials, that systems like AlphaFold have shown you can make progress on. And fusion, we actually did some work with the Swiss Plasma Center at EPFL, using reinforcement learning to control the plasma in a tokamak, to hold it in these configurations that are very hard to maintain with classical controllers. So it's a plasma control problem, a materials problem, and a design problem, and all three are amenable to the kinds of tools we're building.

I should say I'm not a fan of trying to predict exact timelines. Fusion has famously been thirty years away for sixty years. But I think the confluence of better simulation, better control, and better materials discovery changes the shape of the problem. And if you get abundant clean energy, a lot of other things fall out of it, water desalination, carbon capture becomes economically viable, you lift a lot of constraints on society. So it's one of those root-node problems. If I had to bet on where we end up in, say, fifty years, it's some combination of those two, with everything else being transitional.

r001.rationale: The response mentions better batteries as an area for solar-related progress, but does not identify energy storage as a key bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It mentions superconductors for transmission, but does not clearly identify electricity transmission as a key bottleneck for solar power.

r003.rationale: It describes controlling and maintaining tokamak plasma as difficult, but does not state that sufficiently fast plasma control is a condition for feasible fusion power.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re complementary bets. Solar is something we can deploy now, and there’s still room to improve the efficiency of the panels, the manufacturing, and especially the storage that lets you use that energy when the sun isn’t shining. There’s a lot of scope for AI to help with the materials science behind those things.

Fusion is a longer-term bet, with much greater technical uncertainty, but an enormous upside: abundant, clean energy from a very small amount of fuel. The physics is compelling; the challenge is turning that into a reliable, economical power plant. And there are difficult problems there, from controlling the plasma to developing materials that can withstand those conditions.

What excites me is that energy is an enabling technology for almost everything else. If you can make clean energy abundant and cheap, things like desalination become much more practical. You ease a whole set of constraints on human prosperity. So I wouldn’t claim we know those two will be the whole answer, but they seem like very worthwhile bets.

r001.rationale: It highlights storage as a key area for solar improvement, explaining that storage allows use of solar energy when the sun is not shining.

r002.rationale: It does not mention electricity transmission as a solar bottleneck.

r003.rationale: It names plasma control as a difficult fusion problem but does not specify that control must be sufficiently fast.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as complementary bets. Solar is the nearer-term one: it’s abundant, and the engineering challenge is increasingly about how you capture it cheaply, store it, and get it where it’s needed. Better batteries and better grids are a big part of that picture.

Fusion is a more ambitious bet. We know the underlying physics works—the stars demonstrate that—but making it work reliably and economically here on Earth is an extraordinarily difficult engineering problem. So I wouldn’t assume a particular timeline. But the potential payoff is enormous: abundant, low-carbon power that you can generate whenever you need it.

And what excites me is that AI could help with both. You can use it to search for better materials for solar cells and batteries, and to model and control complex physical systems, which is relevant to fusion. It doesn’t remove the need to build things and run experiments, but it could make that cycle much faster.

Ultimately, cheap, clean energy would relax so many other constraints. Desalination becomes more affordable, for example. So these are bets where even a relatively small improvement in our ability to solve the science could have a very large benefit.

r001.rationale: It says solar’s engineering challenge includes how to store the energy, and calls better batteries part of the picture.

r002.rationale: It says solar energy must be gotten where it is needed and identifies better grids as part of the challenge.

r003.rationale: It mentions AI modeling and controlling complex physical systems relevant to fusion, but does not identify sufficiently fast plasma control as a condition for feasible fusion power.
